question: An idle tab burned a full day's API allowance before anyone noticed — what actually caught that, and how fast would a real cost overrun get flagged now?
This all seems to run through one person as coordinator, reviewer, and the one who flips production — how does a team of several people actually adopt this without becoming a bottleneck?
How were the four persona briefs actually written — real user research distilled into jobs, or just demographics like age and device made up?
What actually stops an unattended overnight agent from merging a change that passes its gate but is wrong in a way the gate didn't anticipate?
Is the 'about 30 minutes a day' anywhere logged with timestamps, or is it entirely recall — and does it include the time spent writing gates and briefs, not just babysitting runs?
Concretely, what does a gate look like when you write it—is it a test script, a threshold number in a config file, or something a human still has to read?
The persona panel said DONE at 21:50 and you found it unusable on your own phone the next morning — how many other DONE verdicts have you not personally re-checked?
The 87-lot ground truth is your own taps from one tapper over five days — what's your inter-rater reliability, and why not a held-out labeler?
If I've never used a worktree before, what's the actual command sequence to spin up a lane, and how does it merge back when the gate passes?
Now that you've seen the panel pass something broken, what's the actual workflow — does a human walk every UI change on a real device before merge, or only after a failure like this one?
What did this actually cost end to end, in dollars and in your own hours, once you count everything beyond the $9 labeling spend buried in the backup slide?
With forty-five or more forks possible for one bug, who or what decides which experiments actually get run first?
The panel said DONE on a fixed viewport and missed rotation and scrolling entirely — what exactly does the panel check, and who wrote those acceptance criteria?
Was top-3 chosen as the bar before you saw the top-1 numbers, or after top-1 came in lower than you wanted?
You call the jitter fixed once thrown-away answers hit near zero — was 'it holds' ever judged by a person watching the screen, or only by the event logs?
The persona panel said DONE but the real app was unusable the next morning — what changed in the gate after that, or could it fail silently again?
Dez going from 30 seconds to 9 seconds a task is simulated, not human — what makes that a usability number at all rather than a model narrating improvement?
Is two in three good enough to ship to real users, and what's the number you're targeting before you'd call this done?
For the persona review gate, who or what actually plays the four personas and returns DONE or NOT—is that a scripted prompt, and how do I stop it from rubber-stamping?
Do these persona panels ever get compared side by side against real usability sessions, or are they only ever checked against your own hands after the fact?
What did the review-screen redesign for labeling actually change on screen, and was that tested against alternatives or just shipped from the persona feedback directly?
For the overnight caps—8 calls, 60 seconds, $6—where do you actually set those, and what stops an agent from just retrying past them?
If a PM on my team doesn't run git worktrees or write gate code themselves, what's the actual first thing they'd do on Monday?
You show four different top-3 numbers from 70 to 82 percent — which one did you actually gate decisions on while running the experiments, in real time?
Letting the swarm self-steer broke the next day — what specifically did it do, and how do you know your fix wasn't just papering over the same failure mode recurring later?
When a usage limit killed three build lanes mid-work, how did you recover those lanes the next morning—rerun from scratch or resume from the last commit?
The language head's dev split for tuning its one knob — was that split drawn from the same distribution as the 201 test photos, or could it share sellers, listings, or lighting conditions with them?
What does 'reviewer one tier up' mean in practice—are you literally pointing a bigger model at a smaller model's diff, and how is that wired up?
Who on your team can decline or override what a persona panel asks for, and does that feedback ever get treated as a hard requirement instead of a signal?
When an unattended overnight run picks the wrong fork, what's the blast radius before a human notices and how do you roll it back?
You raised the per-run caps from 8 calls and $6 to 14 calls after agents hit the wall — who signed off on that, and is there a hard ceiling above which an agent still can't spend more no matter what?
The 45-forks estimate on the fork-tree slide is explicitly your own count and not in the record — how would that number change the ROI story if it were, say, half that?
Who has the authority to make the calls you kept for yourself, like flipping something to production, once this isn't a one-person project anymore?
How many lanes can realistically run in parallel before the coordinator session itself becomes the bottleneck?
When the identify vote misses and gets a card wrong, what does the person actually see — a confident wrong answer, or something that signals uncertainty?
In the starter kit, which file would I open first if I just want to copy the gate-and-flag pattern for my own overnight runs?
You used 'top-3' and 'embedding' without defining them on screen—can you walk through what a top-3 check is actually computing?
What's actually in the starter kit — does it assume the same subscription and tooling you had, or does it work with a normal team stack?
For the 65% top-3 figure on live lots, who decided what counted as 'the right card' — the same one tapper who's judging usability elsewhere in this project?
